label_kinds.DATA-DERIVED FINDING: arithmetic over what the documents print
label_kinds.POSSIBLE CONNECTION: two records share a printed value
label_kinds.UNRESOLVED: the documents raise it and cannot answer it

findings.headline: The folder holds 5 reference documents, and 14 of the rules that decide a tender are printed in them
findings.detail: These are the only statements of procedure in the archive. Everything quoted here is from a PDF in the folder, named with its page. The standard tender document among them is marked on its own first page as a preliminary working draft, and no notice in this archive names the standard document it was written from, so these rules describe the procedure as the supplied copies state it rather than the procedure proved to have governed any particular tender. Some of these pages are set in two columns and the clause heading printed in the margin lands inside the sentence when the text is extracted; the quotes are left exactly as extracted rather than tidied, so a reader who turns to the page sees what the parser saw.
findings.calculation: regex search of raw_pages.json over the documents in eGP_Forensic_Engine/

findings.headline: Both printed tests of whether a price is reasonable need something this archive never prints
findings.detail: The low-price test is run on the prices of the technically responsive tenderers, and the clause says how many it takes: "(at least two tenders)". It weighs those prices against an official cost estimate (2026-01-04-13-47-03-e-PG3A.pdf p30; the sentence on that page is broken by the clause heading printed in the margin). The other test rejects a tender whose evaluated price deviates from that same official estimate by more than twenty percent (2026-01-04-13-47-03-e-PG3A.pdf p31). No tender notice and no award notice in this archive prints an official cost estimate, and none prints a quoted price. So neither test can be re-run from these documents, and where only one tender was responsive the first test cannot have been run as written.
findings.calculation: no column of tenders.csv, contracts.csv or bids.csv carries an official cost estimate or a quoted price

findings.headline: Nothing in the folder sets a minimum number of tenderers for an open tender
findings.detail: A sweep of all 231 reference pages for any phrase that puts a floor under a count of tenders or tenderers returns 1: "at least two tenders", which is the condition on the low-price test rather than a condition on holding the tender. Weak competition appears once as a ground on which a procuring entity *may* end a tender - "there is evidence of lack of effective competition; such as non-participation by a number of potential Tenderers; or (c) the Tenderers are unable to propose completion of" - and the word is may. So a tender awarded on one responsive bid cannot be measured against a printed threshold, because the supplied documents do not state one.
findings.calculation: regex sweep of raw_pages.json over eGP_Forensic_Engine/ for a minimum, at-least or not-less-than phrase governing a count of tenders, tenderers, bids or quotations

findings.headline: The typical tender in this archive was open for 22 days, the shortest for 8 and the longest for 97, and every one of the 1129 that printed both dates was opened on the day it closed
findings.detail: The window is counted from the date the notice says it was published to the date it says tendering closed. Half the archive falls between 16 and 28 days. The tenders were opened the same day they closed in every case, which is what an electronic system does automatically, and the last day a tender document could be bought was a median of one day before closing. Works packages stayed open slightly longer than goods packages - a median of 22 days against 20.
findings.calculation: closing_date minus published_date per row of tenders.csv

findings.headline: One rule in the folder can be re-run against the notices from end to end, and it holds in every case: the tender security must stay valid at least 28 days past the tender's own expiry, and all 1118 notices that print both dates do - 1110 of them by exactly 28 days
findings.detail: The rule is printed at 2026-01-04-13-47-03-e-PG3A.pdf p23: the security shall "remain valid for at least twenty-eight (28) days beyond the expiry date of the Tender Validity in order to make a claim in due course against a T". Both dates it needs are on the face of the notice, so this is the only test on this site where the record answers the rule without anything having to be assumed. Nothing falls short. The margin is not scattered above the minimum either - 99.3% of the notices sit exactly on it, 5 at 30 days and 3 at 90 - which is the signature of a date the portal computes from the rule rather than one an officer picks per tender. That matters for reading everything else here: where this archive can be checked against a printed rule, it checks out. What the rest of this investigation runs into is not a record full of breaches; it is a record that stops before the questions can be asked.
findings.calculation: security_valid_until minus tender_valid_until per row of tenders.csv, compared with the 28 days the quoted rule requires

findings.headline: The folder calls a tender validity period of 60 to 150 days normal; 0 of the 1102 notices that print it fall below 60, and 17 run to 180 days
findings.detail: The same page of the standard tender document that sets the band also says a shorter or longer period "may be authorized by HOPE or Authorized Officer" (2026-01-04-13-47-03-e-PG3A.pdf p39), so a period outside the band is something the rule provides for rather than something it forbids. Four lengths account for almost the whole archive - 120 days in 603 notices, 90 days in 435 notices, 60 days in 42 notices, 180 days in 17 notices - which again reads as a field chosen from a short list rather than computed per tender. No notice prints an authorisation for the 17 that run past the band, and no document in the folder records one, so whether they were authorised is not on the public record.
findings.calculation: tender_valid_until minus closing_date per row of tenders.csv against the band read from the quoted rule

findings.headline: Nothing in the folder says how long a national tender must stay open, and all 1150 of these tenders are national
findings.detail: Every notice in the archive prints its procurement type as NCT - national competitive tendering. The folder prints exactly two figures for how long bidders must be given, both on one page of chapter2_en.pdf: "not less than 45 days shall be allowed for international bidding." and "not less than 90 days shall be allowed to enable prospective bidders to conduct investigations at the site before submitting their bids.". The first is about international bidding and the second about large civil works or complex equipment, and both are prefaced "generally". Neither is a rule for a national tender, so the 22-day median window here cannot be called long or short against anything the folder prints - including the 75 tenders that stayed open two weeks or less. The yardstick is missing from the supplied documents, not from the archive's behaviour.
findings.calculation: procurement_type over tenders.csv; regex search of raw_pages.json over eGP_Forensic_Engine/ for any figure of days allowed for tendering

findings.headline: 160 of the 1150 tender notices carry an amendment, 144 of them printing a table of what changed; of the 735 changes those tables list, 216 print an old value and a new value that are the same
findings.detail: The amendment is printed on the notice itself, so a notice downloaded today shows the amended values and not the ones first advertised. The change table is the only place in the archive where both versions appear. Where a row lists a field but prints the same value twice, the document does not say what about that field changed, and this analysis does not guess: the row is counted as listed and not as a change.

findings.calculation: amendments.csv and amendment_changes.csv, one row per field the notice's change table lists; value_changed compares the printed old and new strings

findings.headline: All 404 date changes the amendment tables print move the date later; none moves it earlier. The 104 changes to a closing date, across 88 tenders, add a median of 7.0 days each
findings.detail: An extension gives everyone who is still watching more time, and the direction is the same in every case the archive prints: not one deadline in the amendment tables was brought forward. The documents do not print who asked for the extension, except in the few notices quoted under F-AMEND-05.

findings.headline: For the 83 amended tenders where both versions can be dated, the bidding window as first advertised was a median of 22 days and the window after amendment a median of 30 days - so the 22-day median this investigation reports for the whole archive is the amended figure, not the one bidders first saw
findings.detail: The closing date in the dataset is the one the notice prints today, which for an amended tender is the extended one. That matters for reading the clock: a short window that was later extended is recorded here at its extended length, so the count of short windows is a floor and not a ceiling. It cannot be corrected in the other direction, because a tender whose window was shortened would show the same way - and no shortening appears in any amendment table.
findings.calculation: published_date from tenders.csv against the old and new closing dates in amendment_changes.csv

findings.headline: In 36 tenders the requirement to enter was rewritten after the notice was published. The change tables print 10 money thresholds in both versions; 7 of them move in a direction that can be read, 6 down and 1 up
findings.detail: This is the one place in the archive where a rule of entry can be read in both versions, so it is the one place where the direction of a change is a matter of record rather than inference. Most of the movement is downward, and the largest of it is a factor of 5.0: tender 100483 cut the turnover a bidder had to show from 20.00 Corers to 4.00 Corers. The 1 that went the other way is tender 174037, which raised the value of the past contract a bidder had to show from 60 Million to 70 Million in a clause that at the same time lengthened the period the contract could have been performed in. Of the 10 thresholds, 5 print a scale word on both sides and can be read as sums; 2 print the same misspelled scale word twice, so the ratio between the two figures is readable and the sums are not; and 3 cannot be paired at all, because the scale word differs between the two sides or the clause holds a different number of figures in each version. Those are left unread rather than guessed at. What none of these notices prints is who asked for the change, or whether any firm had already bought the tender document under the earlier rule.

findings.headline: No amendment in the archive prints the date it was made, and only 16 of the 160 amendment notices print any ground for the change; so whether a rule was rewritten before or after firms bought the tender document cannot be established from these documents
findings.detail: The amendment carries a number - first, second - and a free-text note that is usually a description of the field that moved rather than a reason for moving it. The only place in the whole archive where an amendment date is even provided for is a blank in BPPA's own standard document, which reads "Amendment is [insert effective date] or upon execution whichever is later". The notices as published leave that blank unfilled. The 16 notices that do say something are quoted here in full: two name the pandemic, two name a national election, one of those adding that the tenderers asked for the extra time, and 3 say only that the circumstances were unavoidable. That is the extent of it. The sequence that would matter most - rule published, documents bought, rule changed - cannot be reconstructed, and this investigation does not attempt to.

findings.headline: 545 of the 1150 tender notices print at least one rule of entry a reader can check; 615 print at least one clause that points at a document the portal does not publish, and 10 do both
findings.detail: Every notice in this archive prints an "Eligibility of Tenderer" heading, so nothing is missing from the page. What differs is what follows the heading. 615 clauses across 615 notices say only that the criteria are as per the Tender Data Sheet, the Instructions to Tenderers or the tender document - documents obtainable by buying the tender document, and not among the 1,805 PDFs. For the 605 notices that print nothing else, who was allowed to enter is not on the public record.

findings.headline: Of the 3239 clauses the notices print, 1327 read as ordinary for this archive, 870 set themselves apart in one way, 59 name a particular product, and 22 do two or more of those at once
findings.detail: The labels are defined by the arithmetic printed beside them and carry no finding about anyone's conduct. "Ordinary for this archive" means only that other notices in this same archive ask for the same thing; it is not a statement about what procurement elsewhere asks for. The remaining 961 clauses state no rule that can be measured here.
findings.calculation: one label per row of eligibility_criteria.csv, by the rule in LABEL_MEANING; thresholds compared against the ninetieth percentile of the same kind of figure across the archive

findings.headline: Across the 591 award notices that print bid counts, 3436 documents were sold, 2749 bids arrived, 1752 were found responsive and 591 contracts were signed
findings.detail: Every figure is the sum of a number printed on the award notice itself. The four stages are not four measurements of the same thing: a document may be bought and never used, and a bid may arrive and be set aside before it is evaluated.
findings.calculation: sum of documents_sold, bids_received and bids_responsive over the 591 rows of bids.csv where counts_printed = yes

findings.headline: No supplied document names a single bidder, a single price or a single reason for rejection
findings.detail: The 2749 bids that arrived and the 1752 found responsive are counts only. There is no bidder list, no quoted price, no evaluated amount, no ranking, no score and no per-bidder reason in any of the 1,805 PDFs. Anything about who lost, or why, is outside what these documents can establish.
findings.calculation: bids.csv column bidder_level_data_available is no on every row

findings.headline: 201 of 591 tenders reached the award stage with exactly one responsive bid (34.0%)
findings.detail: A single responsive bid is not in itself irregular - a tender can draw one serious bidder. It does mean the price was not compared with any other price at the moment of award, and in 87 of these the notice records only one bid arriving at all.
findings.calculation: count of rows in bids.csv where bids_responsive = 1

findings.headline: In 256 tenders every bid that arrived was found responsive; in 335 at least one was set aside
findings.detail: The number set aside per tender runs from 0 to 54. The documents print the count and never the ground, so each of these is a question for the procuring entity, not an answer.
findings.calculation: bids_received - bids_responsive, tallied over bids.csv

findings.headline: Sorting the 591 tenders that printed their counts by the strongest clause each one printed does not separate them: the share ending with a single responsive tenderer is 48.0% where a clause matched two or more of the tests and 33.4% everywhere else, a difference this many tenders would produce by chance about 14 times in a hundred
findings.detail: This is the join the investigation exists to test, and it comes back empty. Only 25 of the 591 tenders with printed counts carry a clause labelled RESTRICTIVE-LOOKING PATTERN or HIGHLY SPECIFIC, so the comparison is between a small group and a large one and only a large difference could be read as anything; the two-sided Fisher exact p is 0.137 for ending with one responsive tenderer and 0.683 for dropping anyone at all. Read plainly: in this archive the wording of a rule of entry does not predict how many tenderers were left standing. That is not a finding that the wording had no effect. No notice and no award in these 1,805 PDFs names a single tenderer, prints a quoted price, or gives a reason any tenderer was found non-responsive, so nothing here can connect a particular clause to a particular exclusion in either direction. The counts are the only outcome the record offers, and against the counts the labels do not sort.
findings.calculation: strongest label per tender_id from eligibility_criteria.csv by LABEL_ORDER, joined to bids.csv on tender_id where counts_printed = yes; two-sided Fisher exact test over the 2x2 of strong label against outcome

findings.headline: The folder recommends that the cash a tenderer must hold be 80 to 100 percent of the estimated cost, and 60 to 80 percent for the past contract it must show; measured against the contract value actually signed, the middle of this archive sits at 75 and 70 percent, and 25.5% and 29.2% of tenders sit above the band
findings.detail: Both bands are printed on one page of the standard tender document in the folder (2026-01-04-13-47-03-e-PG3A.pdf p38) and both are advisory: the word is recommended, and the first page of that document calls itself a preliminary working draft. Both measure against the estimated cost of the procurement, and no notice or award in this archive prints an estimated cost, so the comparison here is against the contract value eventually signed - a different quantity, and the nearest one the record offers. That substitution is worth watching, and it is also what makes the result readable: if the signed value were unrelated to the estimate the ratios would fall anywhere, and instead 38 of 239 cash requirements and 66 of 137 past-contract requirements land inside the recommended band, with the middle of each distribution within a few points of it. The tail is where the question sits. 61 cash requirements ask for more than the recommended ceiling, the highest for 3.00 crore taka against a contract of 42.92 lakh taka - 7.0 times the value signed. The documents do not say how any of these figures was arrived at, and nothing here shows a rule was broken: an advisory band is not a limit, and the estimate that the band actually refers to is missing from the record.
findings.calculation: largest readable figure of each category in eligibility_criteria.csv over contract_value_taka in bids.csv, same tender_id, figures below the face-value floor excluded; band read from the quoted rule itself

findings.headline: 20 clauses in 17 notices print a sum of money that cannot be read off the page with certainty, and they are left unread rather than guessed at
findings.detail: A figure in a Bangladeshi tender notice is usually printed twice, once in digits and once in words - "Tk 1.20 [One point Two] Crore" - and the words are what make the digits legible, because the scale word can belong to the digits or stand apart from them. Where the two contradict each other, or where the scale word beside the figure is one letter from a real one and so does not settle which was meant, the amount is recorded exactly as printed and left without a number. These are the 20 such clauses; the printed strings are here in full so a reader can judge them: "Tk. 23(Twenty three)"; "Tk. 3(Three)"; "50.00 (fifty ) Lac"; "Tk 2 (Two)"; "Tk 2 (Two)"; "Tk 25 (Twenty) Lacs"; "25 (Twenty) Lacs"; "Tk. 4 (Four) crore". Each is excluded from every distribution and every threshold on this site, and the clause itself is still counted and still classified on everything else it prints.
findings.calculation: eligibility_criteria.csv where money_unresolved = yes; the reason for each is in money_reading

findings.headline: Of the 1150 tender notices, 700 say a contract was awarded, 135 were re-tendered or are to be, 46 were rejected, 26 cancelled and 183 print no outcome at all
findings.detail: The status is a field on the notice, printed by the portal. It is the only account of the ending that most of these tenders have: 641 of the 700 that say a contract was awarded have an award notice in this archive, and 59 do not, so for those the winner, the value and the bid counts are not on the record here. In the other direction 1 award notice names a tender whose own notice is not in the archive. Two tenders print the status Contract Terminated, and both have an award notice.
findings.calculation: status column of tenders.csv against the presence of a tender_id in contracts.csv

findings.headline: 207 tenders ended without a contract and not one of them prints why
findings.detail: The portal prints an ending - re-tendered, to be re-tendered, rejected, cancelled - and stops. No document in the archive gives a ground for any of them: not a tender that drew no responsive bid, not one annulled for weak competition, not one rejected because every price was too far from an estimate. The folder's own rules name those as things that can happen (R-ANNUL-COMPETITION, R-ALL-NON, R-ESTIMATE), so the categories exist in the procedure and the reasons are simply not published. 135 of these tenders were later re-tendered under the portal's own account, which means the work was still wanted; whether the same firms returned cannot be traced, because no notice in this archive links a re-tender to the tender it replaces.
findings.calculation: tenders.csv where status is Rejected, Cancelled, Re-Tendered or To be Re-Tendered; no column in any table carries a ground for the outcome

findings.headline: 309 firms are named as winners across 645 award notices worth 3723.68 crore taka, and 9 of them - 2.9% - account for half of it
findings.detail: Every figure is the sum of contract values printed on award notices. The largest single share belongs to Spectra Engineers Ltd.: 1067.95 crore taka across 4 contracts, 28.7% of all the money in this archive. 105 firms won more than one contract and 204 won exactly one. The most frequent winner by count is M/S. A. R. Enterprise with 15 contracts worth 19.24 crore taka. A concentrated distribution is what public works procurement normally looks like - a few large contracts dominate any sum of money - so this is the shape of the archive rather than a finding about anyone in it.

findings.headline: 68 of the 309 winning firms won from more than one procuring entity, and one won from 7
findings.detail: A firm winning from several offices is ordinary in itself. It is recorded here because it is the only cross-office trace the archive supports: Momotaj Engineers Ltd. won 10 contracts across 7 procuring entities in Dhaka. Whether the same firms competed against each other in those tenders cannot be answered, because no notice names a bidder who did not win.

findings.headline: 34 of the 309 winning firms declare who owns them, and no person named in those declarations is declared an owner of more than one of them
findings.detail: The archive carries 77 ownership declarations naming 49 people. 58 of them print no designation and 45 print no country. For the other 275 firms - 89.0% of the winners - the award notice names the company and stops, so who stands behind it is not on the public record. The question this investigation would most want to ask of a procurement archive is whether the same people own firms that win from the same office, and on these documents it cannot be asked at all: the ownership layer is 89.0% empty, and within the part that exists no person recurs. One value does recur across two firms - "Others (Each Holding < 10%)" - and it is a placeholder the form prints in place of a name, not a person, so it is excluded here.
findings.calculation: beneficial_owners.csv grouped by owner_name, placeholder values excluded, against the winner count in companies.csv

findings.headline: 10 printed addresses in the archive are shared by more than one named firm; 8 of the 10 involve a joint venture printed at its partner's address
findings.detail: An address is printed on the award notice, so this is the government's own record of where a winner sits. Most of these read plainly: a joint venture is registered at the address of one of the firms inside it, and the notice names the partners in the same string. The 2 that do not involve a joint venture are the ones worth a second look, because in each the two firms are also near-identical in name - DAFFODIL ELECTRIC COMPANY LIMITED / Daffodil Electric Company; Super Star Renewable Energy Limited / Superstar Renweable Energy Ltd (SSG Solar) - so the shared address is independent evidence that the pair may be one firm printed two ways. This analysis still does not merge them, because merging on resemblance is how a dataset invents a company; the pair is recorded and left for someone who can check the register.

findings.headline: 219 pairs of names in this archive resemble each other closely enough to be worth checking, and 0 were merged
findings.detail: Two names that look alike are not one entity. 55 pairs differ by at most two characters - "Aliza Enterprise" against "M/S. Maliha Enterprise" is one of them - and 164 have one name's words entirely inside the other, which is what a joint venture's name does to its partner's. Merging either kind on sight would silently rewrite who won what, so every pair is recorded with its measure and none is merged. That decision has a cost, and it is stated here rather than hidden: where a firm is printed two ways, this archive counts it twice, and the contract counts in the money tables are counts of printed names.
findings.calculation: name_candidate_pairs.csv, written by the dataset stage and left unmerged; the audit re-checks that merged is no on every row

findings.headline: 908 of the 1151 tenders carry at least one of the 10 printed observations this investigation can check, and 9 carry four or more
findings.detail: The observations are listed with their definitions beside this finding, and each is either something a document prints or the documented absence of something. The count is not a score and does not rank anyone: the observations overlap heavily - a tender with one responsive bid has usually also set bids aside - and no supplied document finds that any of them was improper. The most frequent is "no rule of entry published" at 612 tenders. The highest count any single tender reaches is 4. What the count is good for is deciding what to read next: the tenders at the top of this list are the ones where the record raises the most questions it does not answer.

label_meaning.COMMON: the subject of this clause is printed by at least a fifth of the notices in this archive, and nothing about it narrows the field further
label_meaning.UNUSUAL: one thing about this clause sets it apart from the rest of the archive - either its subject is printed by fewer than one notice in twenty, or the figure it demands is above the ninetieth percentile of the figures other notices demand for the same thing
label_meaning.HIGHLY SPECIFIC: the clause names a brand, a model, an origin or a manufacturer's authorisation, so it describes a particular product or a particular way of buying it rather than a capacity to do the work
label_meaning.RESTRICTIVE-LOOKING PATTERN: two or more of those things at once. This is an investigative signal about the wording of a clause and nothing more: the documents do not say why any criterion was written as it was, and no supplied document finds that any criterion was improper
label_meaning.UNDETERMINED: the clause states no requirement that can be measured here - it points at a document the portal does not publish, or its subject is not one the parser recognises, or the only figures it prints could not be read from the page

rows.status: no tender notice in the archive

definitions.short: one responsive bid
definitions.means: the award notice records exactly one responsive tenderer

definitions.short: bids set aside with no reason printed
definitions.means: more bids arrived than were found responsive, and no document says why any was set aside

definitions.short: a rule of entry that stands out
definitions.means: at least one eligibility clause is labelled HIGHLY SPECIFIC or RESTRICTIVE-LOOKING PATTERN by the rule in LABEL_MEANING

definitions.short: a demand above the folder's recommended size
definitions.means: a cash or past-contract requirement exceeds the band the standard tender document recommends, measured against the contract value signed

definitions.short: open two weeks or less
definitions.means: fourteen days or fewer between the published date and closing

definitions.short: no rule of entry published
definitions.means: every eligibility clause points at a document the portal does not publish

definitions.short: says awarded, no award notice here
definitions.means: the notice's status is Contract Awarded and no award notice for it is in the archive

definitions.short: counts that cannot all be true
definitions.means: the award notice's own three counts contradict each other

definitions.short: validity longer than normal
definitions.means: the tender validity period exceeds the band the standard tender document calls normal, and no authorisation for it is printed

definitions.short: winner shares an address with another firm
definitions.means: the winner's printed address is printed for at least one other named firm
